merger_description:
Kimberly-Clark Corporation, together with its subsidiaries (**Kimberly-Clark**) proposes to acquire Kenvue Inc. and its subsidiaries (**Kenvue**) (the **Acquisition**).

Kimberly-Clark is a global corporation, headquartered in the United States, which produces and sells personal care products for personal, business and industrial use. Kimberly-Clark’s brands include Huggies, Kleenex, and Viva.

Kenvue is a global corporation, headquartered in the United States, which produces and sells consumer healthcare products. Kenvue’s brands include Band-Aid, Zyrtec and Aveeno.

Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue both supply feminine hygiene (period care) products in Australia, namely tampons, sanitary pads and panty liners under the brands ‘U by Kotex’ (Kimberly-Clark) and ‘Carefree’ and ‘Stayfree’ (Kenvue).

To pre-emptively address potential competition concerns that may otherwise arise from the Acquisition due to the overlap between the parties in the supply of feminine hygiene products, Kimberly-Clark has offered an undertaking pursuant to section 87B of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 which provides for the divestiture of Kenvue's feminine hygiene business in Australia and New Zealand (the **Remedy Offer**).

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: When making a determination in Phase 1, the ACCC undertakes a competition assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Act. In doing so, the ACCC must have regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the interests of consumers. OFFICIAL SENSITIVE

Where the ACCC is satisfied that the acquisition, if put into effect, could, in all the circumstances, have the effect of substantially lessening competition in a market, the ACCC may also consider whether any competition issues can be addressed by one or more conditions.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines and interim merger process guidelines.

In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered the information and documents that were submitted with the notification form, additional information provided by the parties to the acquisition, market feedback and publicly available information.
For the reasons given below, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into effect with conditions.
Overlap and relationship between the Parties

Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue (the Parties) overlap in the wholesale supply of feminine hygiene products (tampons, sanitary pads and panty liners). Kimberly-Clark’s ‘U by Kotex’ and Kenvue’s ‘Carefree’ and ‘Stayfree’ brands are supplied at the wholesale level to supermarkets and other grocery stores, pharmacy wholesalers, discount stores, convenience stores and online retailers.

The Parties also supply products that could be considered complementary, as they fall within a ‘baby care’ product category. Kimberly-Clark supplies the ‘Huggies’ brand of nappies and wipes, and Kenvue supplies both ‘Aveeno’ and ‘Johnson’s’ branded baby toiletries.

The ACCC considers that the Parties’ baby care products are unlikely to raise competition concerns. This is because third party feedback and information received from the Parties indicates that the merged firm would continue to face competition from multiple alternative suppliers of relevant baby care products, and that retail customers typically negotiate with suppliers on a product-by-product basis, rather than by reference to broader categories such as baby care.
Industry background

Feminine hygiene products are used to absorb or collect menstrual blood and principally comprise disposable products including sanitary pads, panty liners, and tampons. Reusable products such as period underwear, menstrual cups/discs and reusable cloth pads comprise a small percentage of feminine hygiene sales in Australia. The Parties’ overlap is limited to disposable products, and they are the focus of this Determination.
Disposable feminine hygiene products are relatively standardised products in terms of their core functionality, with limited scope for meaningful differentiation.
The Parties are both large global suppliers of feminine hygiene products. In Australia, their main customers are supermarkets and pharmacy wholesalers. OFFICIAL SENSITIVE

Third party feedback, including from the retailers of these products, indicates that many consumers of feminine hygiene products have a degree of loyalty to particular brand(s). While consumers do switch, particularly in response to price promotions, it appears that most switching occurs only between the brands owned by the three major suppliers, Kimberly-Clark, Kenvue, and Essity (which supplies feminine hygiene products under the ‘Libra’ and ‘TOM Organic’ brands). Information before the ACCC indicates that this is because these suppliers have built up consumer trust and goodwill over a long period of time and have trusted brands with which Australian consumers are familiar. 3. Competition assessment

The ACCC has considered the effects of the Acquisition by comparing the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition proceeds against the continuation of the current state of competition (being the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition does not proceed).
Relevant areas of competition

The ACCC considers that, for the purposes of assessing the Acquisition, the relevant area of competition is the market for the supply of feminine hygiene products nationally. The bulk of this market is comprised of three product categories: sanitary pads, panty liners and tampons. The positions of the major competitors are similar across each of these product categories, and considering each product category separately would not change the ACCC’s competitive assessment of the Acquisition.

The Parties provided information to the ACCC that indicates they compete closely in relation to the supply of feminine hygiene products in Australia. This position was also supported by market feedback received by the ACCC from third parties including customers and competitors.
Competition effects in the supply of feminine hygiene products

The ACCC is satisfied that, disregarding any conditions the ACCC could include, the Acquisition could, in all the circumstances, have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of feminine hygiene products in Australia.

The ACCC has considered market shares in the feminine hygiene market using information supplied by the Parties, as well as other market data and third-party feedback. Based on the information available, the ACCC considers that the feminine hygiene market in Australia is highly concentrated, with three major suppliers, being Kimberly-Clark, Kenvue and Essity, and a few smaller alternative suppliers.

Following the Acquisition, the number of major feminine hygiene suppliers would reduce from 3 to 2. Essity would be the only remaining major competitor to Kimberly- Clark. The Acquisition would therefore materially increase concentration in an already highly concentrated market.

The ACCC also considers that alternative smaller suppliers would be unlikely to constrain Kimberly-Clark post-Acquisition as they have relatively low market shares, and meaningful new entry, at a scale and in a timeframe sufficient to constrain the OFFICIAL SENSITIVE merged entity, would be unlikely due to the importance of brand trust and familiarity to consumers in this market, as discussed at section 2.12 above.

For these reasons, the ACCC considers that Kimberly-Clark would have the ability to profitably increase prices (including via a reduction in the level or duration of discounted pricing) and/or decrease the quality of feminine hygiene products supplied in Australia post-Acquisition.
Conditions
The ACCC has determined under s51ABZE(1) of the Act that the Acquisition may be put into effect, subject to conditions.

The conditions are: 1. Kimberly-Clark must divest, or cause the divestiture of, the Divestiture Business to a purchaser approved in writing by the ACCC in accordance with a section 87B undertaking accepted by the ACCC. 2. Kimberly-Clark must provide the ACCC with an executed undertaking under section 87B of the Act in respect of the divestiture of the Divestiture Business, in the form at Attachment A of this determination, within five business days of the date of this determination and comply with that undertaking. (together, the Conditions). The term ‘Divestiture Business’ is defined in the section 87B undertaking that Kimberly-Clark must give and comply with pursuant to the Conditions.

In summary, the Divestiture Business comprises Kenvue’s feminine hygiene business in Australia and New Zealand, including the ‘Stayfree’ and ‘Carefree’ brands and accompanying assets and intangible property.

The ACCC must not include conditions unless it is satisfied that, disregarding any conditions the ACCC could include, the Acquisition, if put into effect, could, in all the circumstances, have the effect of substantially lessening competition in any market.

The ACCC must have regard to all relevant matters, and may have regard to the effect on the interests of consumers that compliance with the conditions would have, or be likely to have, or any consumer benefits that would result, or be likely to result from compliance with the conditions.

It is a contravention of section 45AZ of the Act for a person to put the Acquisition into effect and to not comply with any conditions. Where a person does not comply with conditions, the Federal Court may make orders including, in some circumstances, divestiture or a declaration that the acquisition is void.
Assessment with the Conditions

As set out above, the ACCC is satisfied that, disregarding any conditions, the Acquisition could, in all the circumstances, have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the supply of feminine hygiene products in Australia. To address this, the ACCC has decided to include the Conditions in its determination. OFFICIAL SENSITIVE
The objective of the Conditions is to address the competition issues identified in respect of the Acquisition, as set out in this determination and statement of reasons.
The Conditions incorporate a remedy offer Kimberly-Clark made to the ACCC on 28 July 2026.
The Conditions addresses the competition issues

The Conditions address the competition issues detailed above by preserving the presence in the relevant market of a third major supplier with known and trusted brands that are attractive to Australian consumers. The Conditions do this by facilitating the entry or expansion of an independent competitor through the divestiture of the Divestiture Business to a purchaser approved by the ACCC.
The Conditions can be effectively implemented

The ACCC has had regard to whether there are risks associated with the implementation of the Conditions that may limit the effectiveness of the Conditions in addressing the competition issues. The ACCC considers the Conditions can be effectively implemented. Composition of the Divestiture Business

The ACCC considers that the Divestiture Business is appropriately configured and that a suitable purchaser may operate it effectively. The ACCC has had regard to third party feedback in reaching this view as well as the nature and terms of the Conditions and the undertaking. Emergence of an appropriate purchaser

Based on submissions provided by the Parties and third-party feedback, the ACCC considers there are suitable potential purchasers available to support a timely and effective divestiture of the Divestiture Business to an ACCC-approved purchaser. Integrity of the Divestiture Business and other considerations

The ACCC considers that the integrity of the Divestiture Business will be protected prior to divestiture, and has taken into account other considerations related to the effective implementation of the Conditions.
The ACCC considers that the integrity of the Divestiture Business will be appropriately managed, including because the undertaking provides for:

items: the protection of the Divestiture Business by Kimberly-Clark prior to divestiture,
the appointment of an ACCC-approved independent manager to manage the Divestiture Business prior to divestiture, and
the appointment of an ACCC-approved independent auditor to monitor and report on compliance with the undertaking. OFFICIAL SENSITIVE 4. Applications for review and public benefit

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: applications
Applications for review

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s acquisitions register. To confirm whether there has been any application for review, please contact the Australian Competition Tribunal.
Public benefit application

The notifying party may also apply to the ACCC for a determination that the acquisition would be of public benefit. Pursuant to section 51ABZP(2) of the Act, this application must be made no later than 21 calendar days after the ACCC made this determination.
